candidateRows: Schools should require a factual world-religions curriculum while leaving families free to provide additional religious instruction.
The proposal supplies Dennett's practical response to religious diversity and establishes his distinction between factual study and declaring doctrines false.
Dennett specifies the curriculum's scope, defends its compatibility with religious freedom, and rejects D'Souza's published characterization of it.
Broad religious education can preserve benign faith while undermining toxic forms that depend on keeping young people ignorant.
This causal argument connects religious instruction to the prevention of fanaticism and explains why Dennett regards informed comparison as socially protective.
D'Souza's characterization of the curriculum as an effort to eliminate or discredit religion.
Dennett argues that every major religion has dangerous variants, that these rely on enforced ignorance, and that informed faith deserves to survive.
Religions are human inventions resembling languages or music: collective products that continually evolve rather than remain fixed creations.
This directly answers the debate's invention question and provides the evolutionary model through which Dennett explains religious origins and persistence.
After surveying diverse traditions, Dennett describes religions as rapidly arising human productions whose surviving forms change across generations and millennia.
Biological design, human artifacts, and moral systems can all arise through evolutionary processes without requiring a divine recipient of gratitude.
The move offers a naturalistic account of apparent design and moral goodness, addressing phenomena commonly presented as requiring a divine source.
Dennett places organisms, artifacts, institutions, and morality on the tree of life, celebrates their goodness, and says their existence needs no divine addressee.
Darwinian evolution overturns the intuition that complex or valuable things must originate in a still more intelligent and valuable creator.
This is Dennett's principal mechanism for explaining bottom-up design and for rejecting the inference from minds, value, or complexity to a superior mind.
Creationist and D'Souza-style claims that mind, goodness, and designed complexity must descend from a higher intelligent source.
Dennett uses Darwin's inversion to answer maker analogies and rejects the trickle-down assumption that every important product requires a greater antecedent intelligence.
The concept of God has evolved from a concrete humanlike ruler into an increasingly abstract and featureless ground of being.
The historical transformation of the deity concept is offered as direct support for treating God concepts as evolving human constructions rather than stable discoveries.
Dennett contrasts an early warlord-like Yahweh with later abstract theology and argues that the concept has progressively lost concrete identifying features.
Religion is growing globally, as shown by resurgent Hindu devotion and rapidly expanding Christianity in Asia and Africa.
The demographic counterclaim challenges Dennett's framing of religion as declining and supports D'Souza's portrayal of faith as a vigorous worldwide phenomenon.
Dennett's opening demographic claim that major religions are not meaningfully growing and that the nonreligious are growing fastest.
D'Souza cites worldwide religious revival, including examples from India, Africa, Asia, and South Korea, to dispute Dennett's demographic presentation.
A fair curriculum about belief systems should include atheism's historical influence and the mass violence committed by explicitly atheist regimes.
The move contests the neutrality of Dennett's educational framework and argues that secular ideologies must face the same historical scrutiny applied to religion.
Dennett's proposal for comparative religious education and his presentation of dangerous religious belief as a distinctive public threat.
D'Souza proposes adding Darwinism, Nazism, communism, and atheist-regime atrocities to the curriculum as a counterweight to Dennett's treatment of religious harms.
Much religious moral doctrine is open to rational evaluation and may express universal facts about how societies can successfully function.
The argument challenges the exclusion of religious doctrine from factual inquiry and introduces morality as a domain in which theism may make rationally assessable claims.
Dennett's assertion that no point of religious doctrine is agreed upon as straightforward fact by the world community.
Using later commandments as examples, D'Souza distinguishes revelation from moral propositions and argues that the latter can be debated through reason and social consequences.
The Big Bang's implication that matter, space, and time had a beginning provides modern scientific support for a divine creator.
This begins D'Souza's affirmative evidential case for theism and connects a central cosmological discovery to the theological claim of creation beyond time.
D'Souza contrasts older scientific challenges to theism with Big Bang cosmology, then argues that modern physics corroborates Augustine's claim that time began with creation.
The life-permitting precision of the universe's constants is more simply explained by deliberate design than by self-creation.
This supplies the principal fine-tuning argument offered as rational support for a real creator rather than a humanly invented deity.
After completing an inherited discussion of Augustine and cosmic beginnings, D'Souza introduces precise physical constants and argues that their life-permitting values indicate design.
The rational order of nature and the human capacity to comprehend it are jointly explained by divine rationality and creation in God's image.
The move develops an independent theistic explanation from natural law and human reason, extending the case beyond fine-tuning alone.
D'Souza argues that science uncovers intelligible laws, questions whether evolution alone explains truth-directed reason, and invokes a rational creator as a unified explanation.
Consciousness, intentional choice, and moral responsibility cannot be adequately reduced to deterministic material processes.
This is the central consciousness and free-will argument for a nonmaterial dimension of persons, directly bearing on the stated motion.
Dennett's materialist account of consciousness, agency, and human rationality as products of natural processes.
D'Souza distinguishes persons from mechanically determined objects, argues that deliberation presupposes genuine choice, and links determinism to difficulties for debate and moral accountability.
A cosmic beginning does not establish a creator, because positing God repeats rather than resolves the demand for an origin.
The move directly contests the claimed inference from the universe's beginning to God and challenges the explanatory value of a creator.
D'Souza's claim that the Big Bang and the beginning of space and time support inference to a divine creator.
Dennett accepts that this universe's space and time began with the Big Bang but denies that this entails creation by God, whose own existence would remain unexplained.
Observers necessarily find themselves in a universe compatible with observers, so apparent fine-tuning does not require intelligent design.
This is Dennett's direct central answer to the fine-tuning argument identified in the motion as support for a divine creator.
D'Souza's contention that life-permitting cosmic constants are improbable without the deliberate design of a creator.
Dennett argues that beings like us could not occupy a universe with incompatible laws and invokes possible other universes and anthropic selection instead of design.
Darwinian explanations of free will, consciousness, choice, and intentionality cannot be dismissed merely by asserting that such explanations are impossible.
The reply defends the availability of naturalistic accounts for the consciousness and agency phenomena offered as evidence against materialism.
D'Souza's assertion that Darwinian materialism cannot explain consciousness, intentionality, free choice, or moral agency.
Dennett concedes that a full account cannot be presented briefly but says substantial explanatory work exists and characterizes categorical impossibility claims as unsupported assertions.
Because all of nature began with the universe, its beginning requires a cause beyond nature, which the theistic argument identifies as God.
This is D'Souza's explicit cosmological syllogism connecting the universe's beginning to a supernatural cause identified as God.
Dennett's objection that the Big Bang created space and time without establishing any separate divine creator.
D'Souza argues that a natural explanation cannot account for the origin of all nature, then infers a cause from the universe's beginning and names that cause God.
Fine-tuning concerns the parameters of the whole universe, and speculative multiverse proposals require substantial faith while leaving divine explanation viable.
The move clarifies and defends the debate's principal fine-tuning case while directly challenging the naturalistic alternative offered against design.
Dennett's anthropic and multiverse response that observer selection removes any need to explain fine-tuning through intelligent design.
D'Souza says the relevant precision applies throughout the cosmos, portrays multiverse accounts as speculative, and argues that natural laws still invite an ultimate divine explanation.
Multiple testable natural explanations could account for fine-tuning, whereas an intelligent creator adds an even more extraordinary unexplained entity.
This directly answers both the inference from unexplained laws to God and the claim that speculative cosmology leaves design as the best explanation.
D'Souza's argument that natural laws require an ultimate explanation and that speculative alternatives make a divine explanation comparatively reasonable.

Dennett distinguishes scientific laws from commands, treats proposed cosmologies as testable possibilities, accepts uncertainty, and argues that invoking a creator generates a harder explanatory problem.
Humans can develop morality through shared rational deliberation, and changing moral standards show that divine instruction is neither necessary nor operative.
The move supplies the central secular-morality answer to the motion's claim that objective or workable morality rationally supports a real God.
D'Souza's broader claim that materialist atheism undermines morality, responsibility, and the transcendent basis needed for human values.
Dennett rejects the inference from atheism to moral nihilism, notes that human representatives mediate alleged divine commands, and grounds moral progress in open collective reasoning.
Many conflicts attributed to religion are fundamentally disputes over land, political rule, and self-determination rather than religious doctrine.
This directly contests the claim that religion is a major source of violence by offering an alternative causal account of prominent conflicts.
Dennett's opening emphasis on toxic religion and the harms attributed to religious belief.
D'Souza moves from his account of Christian moral influence to challenge examples commonly invoked as evidence that religion causes political violence.
Religious experience deserves serious evidential consideration because it is widespread and directly experienced, rather than dismissible through isolated comparisons with delusion.
The move supplies a direct epistemic defense of religious experience and challenges the debate's proposed treatment of religion as an invented phenomenon.
Dennett's proposal for comparative religious education and his skeptical treatment of reported religious experience.
After criticizing new-atheist treatment of religion, D'Souza compares inward religious knowledge with personal knowledge of innocence despite contrary external evidence.
A creator of nature exists at a different causal level from events within nature and therefore need not be explained by the physical laws governing the created universe.
This addresses the central regress objection to a divine creator and explains why the proposed creator is not subject to the universe's internal causal rules.
The audience objection that positing a creator merely raises the further question of who created that creator.
In response to a creator-regress question, D'Souza distinguishes causation within a novel from the author's causation of the novel as a whole.
Invoking creation outside nature is self-contradictory because the concept of creation derives its meaning from regularities observed within the natural world.
The reply attacks the coherence of the supernatural-cause argument by arguing that it selectively exports causal language while denying its natural basis.
D'Souza's claim that a supernatural creator causes the universe from outside the laws and causal relations internal to nature.
Dennett argues that D'Souza cannot infer an external creator from natural causal concepts and then declare those concepts inapplicable outside nature.
Disagreement among religions does not rationally justify rejecting them all, just as widespread disagreement about scientific truths would not eliminate the correct answer.
The argument rebuts religious pluralism as a route to atheism and preserves the rational possibility that one religion makes true claims.
The contention that mutually competing religions undermine Pascal's wager and make agnosticism or atheism the rational option.
After acknowledging that religions make mutually exclusive claims, D'Souza compares religious disagreement with cross-cultural disagreement over established scientific propositions.
Demanding objective proof of God imposes a selective standard because ordinary belief in the external world, other minds, morality, and consciousness also begins in subjective experience.
This is a direct epistemological defense of theistic belief, arguing that its experiential basis is not uniquely deficient compared with indispensable ordinary beliefs.
The audience concern that defining God beyond human observation and testing makes God an excessively easy and unfalsifiable answer.
D'Souza elicits concessions about sensory mediation and other minds before arguing that consciousness is the irreducible starting point for access to reality.
Consciousness is not irreducible because scientific inquiry can pool experience, study subjectivity, formulate theories, and increasingly explain its underlying machinery.
The move rejects a key premise of D'Souza's epistemic defense and supports a naturalistic account of a phenomenon offered as resistant to scientific reduction.
D'Souza's assertion that consciousness is an irreducible starting point underlying every human experience of external reality.
Dennett accepts that experience is each person's starting point but argues that shared scientific methods allow consciousness itself to become an object of explanation.
Concepts of God are products of deliberate or culturally evolved human design, much as religions, languages, and other cultural systems acquire design without a conscious designer.
This directly advances the proposition that God is a human invention by supplying cultural evolution as the mechanism generating apparently designed religious concepts.
Dennett distinguishes deliberately contrived religions from historically evolved traditions and treats both as outcomes of human cultural design processes.
The human origin of a concept does not show that its object is unreal, while evolution of life's parts does not eliminate the need for intelligent explanation of the universe as a whole.
The move directly counters the human-invention thesis and restates the cosmological design case while distinguishing it from opposition to biological evolution.
Dennett's argument that concepts of God and religious traditions arose through deliberate or culturally evolved human design.
D'Souza compares God concepts with scientific laws that describe independent reality, then argues that evolution within the universe cannot explain the universe's existence.
Human free will is consistent with creation by a freely choosing God, and evolutionary accounts of reciprocal or kin-based altruism fail to explain substantial disinterested morality.
The response connects divine creation, human freedom, and objective moral agency while challenging the adequacy of evolution as a complete account of morality.
The audience objection that D'Souza inconsistently invokes universal cause and effect while treating human choices as exempt from causal determination.
D'Souza grounds human freedom in resemblance to a freely creating God, accepts evolution for the material body, and disputes evolutionary explanations of selfless conduct.
Evolutionary research can explain the genesis of morality, while deciding which inherited dispositions to endorse remains a political rather than scientific task.
This directly defends the naturalistic account of morality against a principal theistic objection while distinguishing descriptive origins from normative justification.
D'Souza's claim that evolutionary accounts explain only a small fraction of genuinely altruistic morality.
D'Souza had argued that reciprocity and kin selection cannot plausibly explain impartial sacrifice; Dennett answers during the designated response segment.
Religion historically scaffolded valuable social institutions, but secular societies can preserve those achievements after outgrowing the religious framework.
The argument concedes religion's historical contribution while maintaining that its continued supernatural authority is unnecessary, directly advancing the human-invention side.
The question whether highly secular Scandinavian societies undermine claims that religion is needed for social flourishing.
An audience member cites Scandinavian countries as highly secular yet socially successful; Dennett uses a scaffolding analogy to explain that result.
Secular culture cannot safely discard belief in God while retaining moral equality, dignity, and compassion because those values depend on Christian roots.
This challenges the viability of secular morality by arguing that its prized commitments are inherited from and remain dependent upon Christianity.
Dennett's claim that modern secular societies can retain Christian-derived achievements after abandoning religion.
After Dennett presents religion as dispensable historical scaffolding, D'Souza invokes Nietzsche and ancient social practices to dispute that separation.
What deserves commitment under the name of God may simply be naturally occurring human goodness rather than a supernatural being.
This supplies a positive naturalistic reinterpretation of religious language, preserving moral aspiration while rejecting the need for supernatural ontology.
The audience proposal that the goodness Dennett affirms might itself be understood as God.
A questioner asks whether belief in goodness could amount to belief in God; Dennett accepts the value while naturalizing its source.
Human beings have intrinsic cognitive and sensory limits, so reason should recognize its bounded reach rather than presume unrestricted access to reality.
The argument underwrites the theistic case against dismissing transcendent reality merely because human observation and understanding cannot fully encompass it.
The charge that positing an incomprehensible God discourages inquiry and repeats the limited perspective D'Souza attributed to atheists.
A questioner accuses D'Souza of making divine mystery an impediment to inquiry; he answers by eliciting concessions about animal and human limitations.
Scientific inquiry institutionalizes serious doubt about being wrong, whereas religious communities often discourage believers from questioning their faith.
This makes openness to correction a comparative epistemic advantage of scientific naturalism and turns an objection about atheist error against religious certainty.
The audience challenge asking Dennett to confront the possibility that his atheistic position is mistaken.
Asked what happens if he is wrong, Dennett says he has considered that possibility and argues that religious believers should do likewise.
A strict parsimony rule accepting only definitional or empirically verified claims defeats itself because the rule meets neither of its own tests.
This attacks the proposed evidential standard for rejecting God by arguing that the standard is internally inconsistent and therefore cannot exclude theism.
The audience argument that parsimony requires rejecting God's existence absent inductive or deductive evidential support.
A questioner compares God with unevidenced invisible entities and invokes parsimony; D'Souza responds by testing that principle against itself.
The placebo effect indicates that mental states can causally affect bodily matter, so one-way material determination of consciousness should not be assumed.
The argument resists reducing consciousness and agency to physical causation, preserving a nonmaterial dimension central to D'Souza's account of human beings.
The questioner's suggestion that thoughts and decisions are determined by the same physical laws governing neurons.
An audience member asks why brain processes do not entail physical determination of the mind; D'Souza answers with bidirectional mental and material causation.
The Christian intellectual tradition centrally practices humility, questioning, and openness to truth rather than the self-satisfied certainty attributed to believers.
This rebuts a comparative epistemic criticism of religion and claims that the questioning spirit associated with science partly arose from Western Christianity.
Dennett's claim that religious communities discourage doubt and display greater epistemic arrogance than scientists.
Following Dennett's contrast between scientific self-correction and religious certainty, D'Souza appeals to biblical and theological traditions of humility.
Evolution is valid within limits but cannot presently explain life's origin, consciousness, or morality, so atheism should not be presented as a scientific conclusion.
This closing argument accepts biological evolution while denying that its explanatory reach establishes metaphysical naturalism, directly defending rational space for God.
Dennett's repeated accusation that D'Souza caricatures evolutionary explanations and the scientific work supporting them.
In his final extended response, D'Souza appeals to criticism of expansive Darwinian explanations and separates limited evolutionary science from atheistic metaphysics.
